warmup.q: You want every @Inventory class to get a member function inventoryCard() inside the class, so Java callers can write lamp.inventoryCard(). Which tool can do it?
options: A KSP processor that writes the class again with the function inside
A KSP processor that writes an extension function
kapt, because Java processors can add methods
warmup.why: A member inside the class means changing a class you wrote, and only a compiler plugin changes what the compiler writes for your classes. A processor that writes the class again gets a Redeclaration error, as section 2 shows. An extension function works from Kotlin and compiles to a static method that Java calls as LampInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(lamp), not as a member. Java processors have the same limit as KSP.

opening:
Picture moving day itself, with a different person for each kind of job. A helper with a clipboard writes new cards from the labels. A mover opens a box and repacks it. Someone at the new house unpacks a box and checks what's inside. And one older helper reads only labels written in Java, so every label is copied out for that helper first.

Eight lessons have been about the helper with the clipboard, and the last one proved that the helper's cards are right. That leaves the question a newcomer to KSP asks first and an experienced team asks too late: is a processor the right tool for this job at all? The easy trap is to answer from habit, or from a benchmark someone quoted, instead of from the job.

In this lesson, we'll measure generated cards against reflection, find the jobs a processor can't do, port a Java processor to KSP, and meet KSP2 on several platforms at once. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with moving day and a person for each kind of job. The measurements said reflection is fine for a few cards and generated code wins when the work repeats. A processor that tried to repack a box met a second Lamp, kapt turned out to be a photocopier, and the port matched javac byte for byte.

In your own build, list every kapt( line, and check each library's docs for a KSP artifact.

Next, in this part's capstone, the helper writes the moving-day plan the night before: code that builds a program's objects and hands each one what its constructor asks for, generated at compile time. Who works out that the route comes before the driver, and the driver before the truck?

sections.h: Reflection or generated cards: what the numbers say
sections.html:
Reflection is a program inspecting its own classes while it runs: finding a class's fields, reading their values, calling methods by name. Lesson 1 wrote MoveMate's card that way, and lesson 7 generated the same card during the build. Lesson 9's playground puts the two side by side, plus a third version that gives reflection its best shot by looking up each class's fields once and keeping them. Here is the plain reflection card:

Java
static String reflectionCard(Object thing) throws IllegalAccessException {
    Class<?> type = thing.getClass();
    if (!type.isAnnotationPresent(Inventory.class))
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(type.getSimpleName() + " has no @Inventory");
    StringJoiner pairs = new StringJoiner(", ");
    for (Field field : type.getDeclaredFields()) {
        if (Modifier.isStatic(field.getModifiers()) || field.isSynthetic()) continue;
        field.setAccessible(true);                       // open the box
        pairs.add(field.getName() + "=" + field.get(thing));
    }
    return type.getSimpleName() + ": " + pairs;
}
Kotlin
fun reflectionCard(thing: Any): String {
    val type = thing.javaClass
    require(type.isAnnotationPresent(Inventory::class.java)) { "${type.simpleName} has no @Inventory" }
    val fields = type.declaredFields.filter { !Modifier.isStatic(it.modifiers) && !it.isSynthetic }
    return type.simpleName + ": " + fields.joinToString(", ") { field ->
        field.isAccessible = true                        // open the box
        "${field.name}=${field.get(thing)}"
    }
}

The generated card is what lesson 7's processor wrote: MovingDayList.cardFor(thing), a when with one branch per class and a string template per card. The program CardTiming checks correctness first, then measures. It times the first call of each way in a fresh JVM, with the classes the JVM loaded for it, then a million calls of each after a warm-up. On our machine, four cores busy with other builds, it printed:

first call, generated:  34.55 ms, 116 classes loaded -> Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null
first call, reflection:  25.45 ms, 114 classes loaded -> Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null
all three ways agree on all 4 cards: true
generated    119 / 38 / 47 ns per card
reflection   313 / 273 / 267 ns per card
cached       197 / 192 / 178 ns per card

And with the first calls the other way round, -Pargs=reflection-first:

first call, reflection:  33.17 ms, 136 classes loaded -> Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null
first call, generated:  23.46 ms,  95 classes loaded -> Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null

The first calls surprised me. I expected reflection to pay a lot at its first call. It pays a little: in the same position, about 20 more classes and a few more milliseconds. Both ways pay 20 to 35 ms and about a hundred classes for their first card, whichever goes first. The class log says what most of them are: java.lang.invoke classes, the machinery the JVM uses to link a string template the first time it runs. The way that goes second still loads about a hundred, so each new kind of template seems to pay for its own. With four small classes, the first call can't tell the two ways apart. The Part 4 capstone showed where start-up does tell. Its container wired a program's objects by reflection, and it loaded more than twice as many classes as the same wiring written out as plain code.

The warm numbers are steady across runs. A generated card costs about 45 ns; reflection's best shot about 190 ns, four times as much; plain reflection about 280 ns, six times. Lesson 1 saw the same gap between its hand-written card and reflection. Either way, it's a fifth of a microsecond. Nobody at the new house waits for that, unless the program prints a million cards.

So reflection is fine for work that runs a few times, on a few classes: a debug screen, a test helper, a small tool reading settings once at start. It also reaches what a processor can't: classes that arrive while the program runs. Generated code wins when the work repeats, and it brings two things the stopwatch doesn't show. A mistake stops the build with a file and line, as in lesson 5, instead of failing on moving day. And programs compiled ahead of time into a single executable need extra setup for every class they reach by reflection, and none for plain code.

Reflection that runs a few times on a few classes is fine. Generate code when the work repeats, or when a mistake should stop the build.

In the picture, reflection is unpacking a box at the new house to see what's inside. The picture breaks on the size of the cost: unpacking takes an afternoon, and reflection a fifth of a microsecond. Speed, though, was never the only question. Some jobs aren't cards at all.

try.title: Time the cards, both ways round
steps: From labs/, run CardTiming with the command below. Before you look, write down which first call you expect to be slower.
Run it again with -Pargs=reflection-first. Which numbers moved with the order, and which stayed with the way?
Run the Java twin, CardTimingJava, once. It calls the cards KSP generated in Kotlin, through MovingDayList.INSTANCE.

code.title: CardTiming.kt
code.html: package workbench.ksp.app.l09 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory // Generated cards (lesson 7's MovingDayList.cardFor, written by KSP in this build) against reflection. // The first call of each way, in this order, then many calls. Run it twice, the second time with the order // swapped, and see which cost moves with the order: // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.CardTimingKt // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.CardTimingKt -Pargs=reflection-first fun main(args: Array<String>) { val ways: Map<String, (Any) -> String> = linkedMapOf( "generated" to MovingDayList::cardFor, "reflection" to ::reflectionCard, "cached" to CachedReflectionCards::card, ) val things = movingDayThings() val lamp = things[1] // 1. the first call of each way: time, and the classes the JVM loaded for it val order = if (args.firstOrNull() == "reflection-first") listOf("reflection", "generated") else listOf("generated", "reflection") val classes = ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean() for (name in order) { val loadedBefore = classes.totalLoadedClassCount val start = System.nanoTime() val card = ways.getValue(name)(lamp) val ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e6 println("first call, %-10s %6.2f ms, %3d classes loaded -> %s".format(name + ":", ms, classes.totalLoadedClassCount - loadedBefore, card)) } // 2. correctness before speed: every way writes the same four cards val agree = things.all { thing -> ways.values.map { it(thing) }.distinct().size == 1 } println("all three ways agree on all ${things.size} cards: $agree") // 3. many calls, after a warm-up: nanoseconds per card, three rounds each val calls = 1_000_000 for ((name, f) in ways) { repeat(200_000) { f(things[it % 4]) } val rounds = (1..3).map { var length = 0L val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until calls) length += f(things[i % 4]).length check(length > 0) (System.nanoTime() - t0).toDouble() / calls } println("%-12s %s ns per card".format(name, rounds.joinToString(" / ") { "%.0f".format(it) })) } }

alt.title: CardTimingJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.ksp.app.l09; import java.lang.management.ClassLoadingMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Function; // The Java twin of CardTiming.kt: Java code calling the cards KSP generated in Kotlin. They compiled to ordinary // classes, so Java sees MovingDayList as a class with an INSTANCE field, and the reflection cards as static methods. // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.CardTimingJava // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.CardTimingJava -Pargs=reflection-first public class CardTimingJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Map<String, Function<Object, String>> ways = new LinkedHashMap<>(); ways.put("generated", MovingDayList.INSTANCE::cardFor); ways.put("reflection", ReflectionCardsKt::reflectionCard); ways.put("cached", CachedReflectionCards.INSTANCE::card); List<Object> things = MoveMateKt.movingDayThings(); Object lamp = things.get(1); List<String> order = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("reflection-first") ? List.of("reflection", "generated") : List.of("generated", "reflection"); ClassLoadingMXBean classes = ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean(); for (String name : order) { long loadedBefore = classes.getTotalLoadedClassCount(); long start = System.nanoTime(); String card = ways.get(name).apply(lamp); double ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e6; System.out.printf("first call, %-10s %6.2f ms, %3d classes loaded -> %s%n", name + ":", ms, classes.getTotalLoadedClassCount() - loadedBefore, card); } boolean agree = things.stream().allMatch(t -> ways.values().stream().map(f -> f.apply(t)).distinct().count() == 1); System.out.println("all three ways agree on all " + things.size() + " cards: " + agree); int calls = 1_000_000; for (var entry : ways.entrySet()) { Function<Object, String> f = entry.getValue(); for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) f.apply(things.get(i % 4)); StringBuilder rounds = new StringBuilder(); for (int r = 0; r < 3; r++) { long length = 0; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < calls; i++) length += f.apply(things.get(i % 4)).length(); if (length == 0) throw new IllegalStateException(); rounds.append(r == 0 ? "" : " / ").append(String.format("%.0f", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / (double) calls)); } System.out.printf("%-12s %s ns per card%n", entry.getKey(), rounds); } } }

try.expect: Every run prints all three ways agree on all 4 cards: true. The first calls cost tens of milliseconds and about a hundred classes each; reflection loads about 20 more than the generated card in the same position (on our run, 136 against 116 when first, 114 against 95 when second). After warm-up, the generated card takes roughly 40 to 70 ns, the cached reflection card roughly 160 to 250 ns, and plain reflection roughly 220 to 400 ns. Your numbers will differ, and the ratios should not move much.

sections.h: Jobs a helper can't do: when the class itself must change
sections.html:
Lesson 1 named KSP's two limits in the docs' words: processors "can't examine expressions or statements, and they can't modify the source code". A newcomer reads that and thinks of a workaround: if a processor can't add a function to Lamp, it can write Lamp again, with the function inside. RepackDemo tries exactly that, and then the way that works:

Java
// The javac way, the same as KSP's: a new file next to the class, never a change to it
public final class LampCards {
    private LampCards() {}

    public static String inventoryCard(Lamp lamp) {
        return "Lamp: name=" + lamp.getName() + ", bulbs=" + lamp.getBulbs() + ", shade=" + lamp.getShade();
    }
}
Kotlin
// What a KSP processor can do: a new file next to the class, with an extension function
fun Lamp.inventoryCard(): String = "Lamp: name=$name, bulbs=$bulbs, shade=$shade"

// What it can't do: give Lamp itself a new member. Writing Lamp again is a second Lamp.
data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) {
    fun inventoryCard(): String = "Lamp: name=$name, bulbs=$bulbs, shade=$shade"
}

KSP lets the processor write the file, because KSP doesn't check what's in new files. The Kotlin compiler then meets two classes with one name:

=== repack Lamp itself: COMPILATION_ERROR
e: LampExtra.kt:3:12 Redeclaration:
data class Lamp : Any
e: Lamp.kt:6:12 Redeclaration:
data class Lamp : Any
=== add a new card next to it: OK
desk.inventoryCard() returns: Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null

That's one lamp too many. A processor's outputs are always new declarations next to yours: an extension function, a builder class, a list. Java's annotation processors have the same limit, which is why the Java twin is a separate LampCards class.

Some jobs need the class itself to change. A compiler plugin is a jar that the Kotlin compiler loads to change what it writes into class files, and lesson 6 of the Advanced Kotlin track met three. all-open removes final from classes a framework must subclass. no-arg adds a constructor that Kotlin code can't see. kotlinx.serialization writes a serializer inside each @Serializable class and a serializer() function on its companion. No processor can do any of those, because each one changes a class you wrote. In the picture, that's the mover who repacks the box. A plugin can do more, and it costs more to trust: kt-06's whole lesson was that the class you read is not the class the JVM loads.

The ecosystem shows the same line from the other side. Arrow Optics, which generates helpers for reading and copying nested data, still ships a KSP processor, but its docs say "Since version 2.3.0, we recommend using the compiler plug-in". With KSP, "you need to have a companion object declaration in each class, even if it's empty. This is due to limitations in KSP itself": the processor can add functions to a companion, but it can't create the companion. Koin is a library that builds a program's objects and hands them out. Its docs say koin-ksp-compiler "is deprecated and will be removed in a future Koin version", and its annotations are now processed by the Koin Compiler Plugin. Kotlin DataFrame deprecated its KSP plugin the same way. All three pages were checked in November 2026.

If the job is to change a class, it's a compiler plugin's job. If it's to write a new file next to the class, it's KSP's.

The figure puts the choice in three questions. The last box is for a helper we haven't met properly yet: the one who reads only Java.

try.title: Repack a box, then write a card next to it
steps: Run RepackDemo. Read both errors: which files do they name, and at which lines?

Open labs/ksp/build/kctfork/demo/l09-repack/ksp/sources/kotlin/movemate/LampExtra.kt. The second compile cleared the folder, so it holds the extension function. Which line would a Java caller write to call it?

code.title: RepackDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.ksp.l09.demo import com.google.devtools.ksp.buildApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.Dependencies import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.Resolver import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessor import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSAnnotated import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSClassDeclaration import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream // A helper who tries to repack a box: this processor wants to give Lamp a member function, so it writes Lamp // again, with the function inside. KSP lets it write the file; the Kotlin compiler then meets two Lamps. // The second compile does the job the KSP way: a new file with an extension function, next to Lamp. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l09.demo.RepackDemoKt fun main() { val lamp = SourceFile.kotlin( "Lamp.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory @Inventory data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) """, ) val repack = "data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) {\n" + " fun inventoryCard(): String = \"Lamp: name=\$name, bulbs=\$bulbs, shade=\$shade\"\n}\n" val extension = "fun Lamp.inventoryCard(): String = \"Lamp: name=\$name, bulbs=\$bulbs, shade=\$shade\"\n" for ((label, body) in listOf("repack Lamp itself" to repack, "add a new card next to it" to extension)) { val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo/l09-repack").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(lamp) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += writer(body) } } val result = compilation.compile() println("=== $label: ${result.exitCode}") result.messages.lines().dropWhile { !it.startsWith("e: ") }.filter { it.isNotBlank() } .forEach { println(it.replace(Regex("file://\\S*/"), "")) } // the folder is a temporary one if (result.exitCode == KotlinCompilation.ExitCode.OK) { val lampClass = result.classLoader.loadClass("movemate.Lamp") val desk = lampClass.getConstructor(String::class.java, Int::class.java, String::class.java).newInstance("desk lamp", 1, null) println("desk.inventoryCard() returns: " + result.classLoader.loadClass("movemate.LampExtraKt").getMethod("inventoryCard", lampClass).invoke(null, desk)) } } } /** A processor that writes `body` into movemate/LampExtra.kt, once. */ private fun writer(body: String) = SymbolProcessorProvider { env -> object : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true enableContextParameters = true } var written = false override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { if (written) return emptyList() val lamp = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory").first() as KSClassDeclaration env.codeGenerator.createNewFile(Dependencies(false, lamp.containingFile!!), "movemate", "LampExtra") .use { it.write("package movemate\n\n$body".toByteArray()) } written = true return emptyList() } } }

try.expect: Repacking fails with COMPILATION_ERROR and two Redeclaration: errors, one in the generated LampExtra.kt at 3:12 and one in your Lamp.kt at 6:12. The extension compiles and prints desk.inventoryCard() returns: Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null. A Java caller writes LampExtraKt.inventoryCard(desk): the extension is a static method of the file's class, and Lamp itself still has no member.

sections.h: When the only helper reads Java: kapt, and moving a library to KSP
sections.html:
Java has had annotation processors, programs that javac runs while it compiles, since Java 6, and the Java world has written many of them. KSP is Kotlin's own way to do that job for Kotlin code. Between the two sits kapt, Kotlin's bridge to Java's processors. The docs say it "generates stub files from Kotlin source code and then runs the Java annotation processors on those stubs". A stub is a Java copy of a Kotlin class's declarations with the bodies emptied out: methods return null; or return 0;, nullability turned into @NotNull annotations, default values gone.

In the picture, kapt is the older helper who reads only Java, so every label in the room is first copied out in Java for that helper. That copying is the slowness. The picture breaks in one place: a person copying labels would keep every word, and stubs lose some, such as default values. The migration guide calls it "expensive" and says it "significantly increases build time". Android's guide adds a detail that matters when you migrate one library at a time: "If a module has any kapt processors remaining, stubs are still generated in that module." The often-quoted "up to 2x faster" comes from the KSP alpha announcement in 2021, where "initial benchmarks with the Room library show that KSP is approximately 2x faster than KAPT". It's one benchmark, from KSP1 days, not a law.

kapt is still the answer for a processor that exists only for Java. Android's Data Binding is one: "KSP support for Data Binding is not planned". When a library ships both, moving to KSP is mostly a change to the build file. The migration guide says: "For most libraries, this replacement is enough":

// build.gradle.kts, before: kapt runs a javac processor on Java stubs of your Kotlin classes
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.21"
    kotlin("kapt") version "2.4.21"
}
dependencies {
    kapt("com.squareup.moshi:moshi-kotlin-codegen:1.15.2")
}
kapt { arguments { arg("movemate.household", "Okafor") } }

// after: KSP reads the Kotlin declarations directly
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.21"
    id("com.google.devtools.ksp") version "2.3.14"
}
dependencies {
    ksp("com.squareup.moshi:moshi-kotlin-codegen:1.15.2")   // the same artifact serves kapt and KSP
}
ksp { arg("movemate.household", "Okafor") }

KSP and kapt can run side by side, so a project can move one library at a time. Many libraries ship both processors in one jar: Moshi's codegen jar holds a javac services file, a KSP services file and the Gradle incremental descriptor.

When the library is your own, migrating means porting the processor, and this lesson's lab does exactly that. The Java team's JavacPackingSlipProcessor writes META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt, one line per @Inventory class with its room and its fields. You port it to KSP, move by move, until the two outputs match byte for byte. Each javac line has a KSP line:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: the given javac processor, Find and Write
for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class)) { ... }

var slip = processingEnv.getFiler().createResource(StandardLocation.CLASS_OUTPUT, "",
        "META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt", classes.toArray(new Element[0]));
try (Writer out = slip.openWriter()) { out.write(text); }
Kotlin
// The KSP port, Find and Write (the Write is given in the lab)
val found = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation(Inventory::class.qualifiedName!!).toList()

codeGenerator.createNewFile(slipDependencies(classes), "META-INF/movemate", "packing-slip", "txt")
    .use { it.write(text.toByteArray()) }

The rest of the mapping is the same kind of swap. element.getKind() != ElementKind.CLASS becomes classKind != ClassKind.CLASS, and messager.printMessage(ERROR, text, element) becomes logger.error(text, symbol). Fields in source order become the primary constructor's properties. type.getAnnotation(Room.class) becomes a KSAnnotation and its arguments, and getOptions() becomes environment.options. Two javac ideas have no twin. Claiming an annotation by returning true doesn't exist in KSP, where every processor sees every symbol. And Gradle's aggregating category for the whole processor becomes Dependencies(aggregating = true, ...) on the one output, as in lesson 7.

Use KSP for every processor that has a KSP version, and keep kapt only for the ones that don't. One kapt processor left in a module keeps the stubs in that module.

One port detail catches people. Kotlin has a kind of class javac never sees, the object, so the port needs an answer for it that the Java processor never needed. KSP's own story, meanwhile, has moved on from the days of that 2021 benchmark.

try.title: Compare the port's slip with javac's
steps: Read JavacPackingSlipProcessor.java, the Java twin below. Find its four moves.
Run PortDemo. It runs the reference KSP port on Kotlin twins of the four classes and prints its slip next to the one javac wrote for the Java twins.
Open labs/ksp/src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l09/java-twins.txt to see how javac's slip was made. Once your port passes the lab, run PortDemo with -Pmine=l09.

code.title: PortDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.ksp.l09.demo import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.kspSourcesDir import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l09.HOUSEHOLD import workbench.ksp.l09.PackingSlipProcessorProvider // Runs the KSP port of the javac packing slip processor on Kotlin classes, then puts its slip next to the one // javac wrote for the Java twins (stored in src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l09/). Reference port by default; // add -Pmine=l09 for yours. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l09.demo.PortDemoKt fun main() { val things = SourceFile.kotlin( "Things.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory import workbench.ksp.annotations.Room @Inventory @Room("hall") data class Box(val label: String, val room: String, val weightGrams: Int, val fragile: Boolean = false) @Inventory @Room("living room") data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Inventory @Room("study") class Bookshelf(val shelves: Int, val books: List<String>) @Inventory data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) """, ) val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo/l09").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(things) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += PackingSlipProcessorProvider() processorOptions += mapOf(HOUSEHOLD to "Okafor") } } val result = compilation.compile() println("exit code: ${result.exitCode}") result.messages.lines().filter { it.startsWith("w: [ksp]") || it.startsWith("e: [ksp]") }.forEach(::println) val ksp = compilation.kspSourcesDir.resolve("resources/META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt") val javac = File("src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l09/javac-packing-slip.txt") println("--- KSP wrote ${ksp.relativeTo(compilation.kspSourcesDir).invariantSeparatorsPath}:") print(if (ksp.exists()) ksp.readText() else "(nothing yet)\n") println("--- javac wrote META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt for the Java twins:") print(javac.readText()) println("--- the same, byte for byte: ${ksp.exists() && ksp.readBytes().contentEquals(javac.readBytes())}") }

alt.title: JavacPackingSlipProcessor.java
alt.html: package workbench.ksp.l09; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.Writer; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import javax.annotation.processing.AbstractProcessor; import javax.annotation.processing.Messager; import javax.annotation.processing.RoundEnvironment; import javax.annotation.processing.SupportedAnnotationTypes; import javax.annotation.processing.SupportedOptions; import javax.lang.model.SourceVersion; import javax.lang.model.element.Element; import javax.lang.model.element.ElementKind; import javax.lang.model.element.Modifier; import javax.lang.model.element.TypeElement; import javax.lang.model.element.VariableElement; import javax.lang.model.util.ElementFilter; import javax.tools.Diagnostic; import javax.tools.StandardLocation; import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory; import workbench.ksp.annotations.Room; /** * Lesson 9, given and read-only: the Java team's packing slip processor, a javac annotation processor * (javax.annotation.processing, part of the JDK since Java 6). For every class annotated @Inventory it writes one * line into META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt: the class name, its room from @Room, and its fields in order. * Your job in PackingSlipProcessor.kt is to port it to KSP, move by move, so Kotlin classes get the same slip. * * In a Java build it would run through Gradle's annotationProcessor configuration, registered in * META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor, and declared aggregating for Gradle's incremental * compile in META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors: * workbench.ksp.l09.JavacPackingSlipProcessor,aggregating */ @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") @SupportedOptions("movemate.household") public class JavacPackingSlipProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { private boolean slipWritten = false; @Override public SourceVersion getSupportedSourceVersion() { return SourceVersion.latestSupported(); } @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { if (slipWritten || roundEnv.processingOver()) return false; Messager messager = processingEnv.getMessager(); String household = processingEnv.getOptions().getOrDefault("movemate.household", "MoveMate"); // 1. Find: every element annotated @Inventory in this round List<TypeElement> classes = new ArrayList<>(); for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class)) { // 2. Check: only classes, with an error on the exact element if (element.getKind() != ElementKind.CLASS) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "@Inventory goes on a class, but " + element.getSimpleName() + " is " + kindWords(element.getKind()), element); continue; } classes.add((TypeElement) element); } if (classes.isEmpty()) return false; classes.sort(Comparator.comparing(c -> c.getSimpleName().toString())); // 3. Read: one line per class, its fields in source order List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>(); for (TypeElement type : classes) lines.add(slipLine(type)); // 4. Write: one resource for all of them; the originating elements tell an incremental build where it came from try { var slip = processingEnv.getFiler().createResource(StandardLocation.CLASS_OUTPUT, "", "META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt", classes.toArray(new Element[0])); try (Writer out = slip.openWriter()) { out.write("# " + household + " packing slip. Generated, do not edit.\n"); for (String line : lines) out.write(line + "\n"); } } catch (IOException e) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "could not write the packing slip: " + e.getMessage()); } slipWritten = true; return false; // don't claim @Inventory: other processors may want it too } /** "Lamp [living room]: name, bulbs, shade" */ static String slipLine(TypeElement type) { Room room = type.getAnnotation(Room.class); List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); for (VariableElement field : ElementFilter.fieldsIn(type.getEnclosedElements())) { if (!field.getModifiers().contains(Modifier.STATIC)) names.add(field.getSimpleName().toString()); } return type.getSimpleName() + " [" + (room == null ? "no room" : room.name()) + "]: " + String.join(", ", names); } /** The same words the KSP port uses for each kind of declaration. */ static String kindWords(ElementKind kind) { return switch (kind) { case INTERFACE -> "an interface"; case ENUM -> "an enum"; case ANNOTATION_TYPE -> "an annotation"; case RECORD -> "a record"; default -> "a " + kind.name().toLowerCase(); }; } }

try.expect: Both slips read # Okafor packing slip. Generated, do not edit., then Bookshelf [study]: shelves, books, Box [hall]: label, room, weightGrams, fragile, Lamp [living room]: name, bulbs, shade and Plant [no room]: kind, potLitres, waterEveryDays, and the last line is --- the same, byte for byte: true. With an unfinished port, the demo prints w: [ksp] l09 not done yet: ..., (nothing yet) and false.

aside.title: Which libraries ship a KSP processor today?
aside.html: These were checked in November 2026. Room 3.0, Android's database library, is KSP only: "configuration of annotation processor via KAPT or JavaAP is no longer possible in Room 3.0", while Room 2.x still supports javac, kapt and KSP. Dagger and Hilt, which wire a program's objects at compile time, say "Dagger's KSP support is stable as of Dagger 2.60+ and KSP 2.3.9+", although kotlinlang's own table of libraries still calls Dagger "Alpha". kotlin-inject does the same job and has been KSP only since 0.9.0. Moshi's codegen, which writes JSON adapters, serves kapt and KSP from one jar. Tables go stale, so check each library's own docs before you migrate.

sections.h: Several houses at once: KSP2, versions and multiplatform
sections.html:
The KSP in this track is KSP2, and it differs from older articles in ways that matter. Since KSP 2.3.0, KSP2 is the only kind: setting ksp.useKSP2=false fails the build with "KSP1 is no longer available. Please use KSP2 instead". KSP2 "is no longer a compiler plugin". It runs inside the Gradle daemon, the long-lived Gradle process, so a big project may need more heap there, and KSP's docs suggest settings such as org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4096M. Its version number is no longer tied to Kotlin's: this track builds with Kotlin 2.4.21 and KSP 2.3.14. A version written like 2.2.21-2.0.5, Kotlin's number and then KSP's, is the old scheme. The API moved too. KSP 2.3.12 deprecated KSVisitorVoid() and validate() without arguments, the spelling of the official quickstart, and 2.3.14 added the apiFeatures property that every lab in this track overrides.

The last setting is several houses at once. Kotlin Multiplatform is one project compiled for several platforms, such as the JVM, JavaScript and native code, from shared code and code for each platform. Each platform is a target, and each target compiles separately. So KSP runs once per target, with a task and a configuration each:

// build.gradle.kts of a multiplatform module: one KSP configuration per target
kotlin {
    jvm()
    js { browser() }
}
dependencies {
    add("kspCommonMainMetadata", project(":processor"))   // the shared code
    add("kspJvm", project(":processor"))                  // the JVM target: task kspKotlinJvm
    add("kspJs", project(":processor"))                   // the JavaScript target: task kspKotlinJs
    // ksp(project(":processor")) here fails the build:
    // The 'ksp' configuration is deprecated in Kotlin Multiplatform projects.
    // Please use target-specific configurations like 'kspJvm' instead.
}

The plain ksp(...) configuration is right in the single-platform builds of this track. In a multiplatform module it's an error since KSP 2.3.12: you name the targets that need the processor. Each target's output goes to its own folder, such as build/generated/ksp/jvm/jvmMain/kotlin. A class in the shared code gets its card once per target: a run with a JVM and a JavaScript target wrote one in each of metadata/commonMain, jvm/jvmMain and js/jsMain. Koin names "a KSP configuration per Kotlin Multiplatform target" among its reasons for moving to a compiler plugin.

In the picture, it's a family moving into two houses on the same day. Each house gets its own helper, its own pass through the boxes, and its own set of cards, even for the boxes both houses share. The picture breaks only in the counting: in a build, the shared boxes are read once more for the shared code itself.

In a multiplatform module, add the processor to each target that needs it. Plain ksp(...) is for single-platform modules.

That's the last piece of the toolbox. What's left is to use it on a job big enough to need all of it.

compare.title: The packing slip processor: the javac original and its KSP port, move by move

java.title: JavacPackingSlipProcessor.java (excerpt)
java.html: // The given javac processor (javax.annotation.processing) @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") @SupportedOptions("movemate.household") public class JavacPackingSlipProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { private boolean slipWritten = false; @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { if (slipWritten || roundEnv.processingOver()) return false; String household = processingEnv.getOptions().getOrDefault("movemate.household", "MoveMate"); List<TypeElement> classes = new ArrayList<>(); for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class)) { // 1. Find if (element.getKind() != ElementKind.CLASS) { // 2. Check messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "@Inventory goes on a class, but ...", element); continue; } classes.add((TypeElement) element); } // 3. Read: slipLine(type) reads the fields and @Room // 4. Write: filer.createResource(CLASS_OUTPUT, "", "META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt", elements) slipWritten = true; return false; // claim nothing } }

kotlin.title: PackingSlipProcessor.kt (the given part)
kotlin.html: class PackingSlipProcessor( private val codeGenerator: CodeGenerator, private val logger: KSPLogger, private val options: Map<String, String>, ) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } private var slipWritten = false fun processSlip(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { if (slipWritten) return emptyList() // javac: if (slipWritten || processingOver()) val household = options[HOUSEHOLD] ?: "MoveMate" // javac: getOptions().getOrDefault(...) val classes = findInventory(resolver) // 1. Find .mapNotNull { checkKind(it, logger) } // 2. Check .sortedBy { it.simpleName.asString() } if (classes.isEmpty()) return emptyList() val lines = classes.map(::slipLine) // 3. Read val text = "# $household packing slip. Generated, do not edit.\n" + lines.joinToString("") { "$it\n" } codeGenerator.createNewFile(slipDependencies(classes), "META-INF/movemate", "packing-slip", "txt") .use { it.write(text.toByteArray()) } // 4. Write slipWritten = true return emptyList() // deferred symbols: none } }

compare.note: The two processors make the same moves in the same order, which is what makes a port a matter of swapping lines rather than redesigning. The differences are in the contract around them. javac creates the processor with a no-argument constructor and calls process with the annotations it may claim; returning true claims them, and KSP has no claiming at all. KSP creates the processor through a provider and gets back a list of symbols to defer, which javac has no word for. javac runs one more, empty round with processingOver() true; KSP calls finish() instead. And the incremental category moves from the processor (Gradle's descriptor file) to the output (Dependencies).

worked.title: Pick the tool for MoveMate's next four jobs

steps.say: Job 1: a debug screen that prints every field of whatever object a tester taps, a few times a day. It runs rarely and must work for classes nobody annotated. Reflection is fine, and a processor would only add a module and a test suite.
steps.code: static String debugPrint(Object thing) throws IllegalAccessException { StringJoiner parts = new StringJoiner(", ", thing.getClass().getSimpleName() + "(", ")"); for (Field f : thing.getClass().getDeclaredFields()) { if (Modifier.isStatic(f.getModifiers())) continue; f.setAccessible(true); parts.add(f.getName() + "=" + f.get(thing)); } return parts.toString(); }

alt.html: fun debugPrint(thing: Any): String = thing.javaClass.declaredFields .filter { !Modifier.isStatic(it.modifiers) } .onEach { it.isAccessible = true } .joinToString(", ", "${thing.javaClass.simpleName}(", ")") { "${it.name}=${it.get(thing)}" }

steps.say: Job 2: save every box to a file as JSON and read it back, thousands of times a day. The serializer belongs inside each class, with a serializer() function on its companion: that changes classes you wrote, so it's the kotlinx.serialization compiler plugin from the Advanced Kotlin track. In Java you'd reach for a library that reads annotations by reflection.
steps.code: @Serializable data class Box(val label: String, val room: String, val weightGrams: Int, val fragile: Boolean = false) val json = Json.encodeToString(Box("books", "study", 12_000)) // the plugin wrote Box's serializer

alt.html: // Java's usual approach: a JSON library such as Jackson, which reads the class by reflection String json = new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(new Box("books", "study", 12_000, false));

steps.say: Job 3: wire the moving-day crew, where each class asks for what it needs in its constructor, and a missing part should stop the build. The wiring is new code next to your classes, written from their constructors: a KSP processor, and the next capstone builds it.
steps.code: class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver) // the processor writes a factory for Truck // and a component that builds Driver before Truck, checked during the build

alt.html: public class Truck { private final Driver driver; @Inject public Truck(Driver driver) { this.driver = driver; } // a javac processor writes the factory }

steps.say: Job 4: a module uses a processor that exists only as a javac processor, with no KSP artifact. Keep it on kapt for now, move every other library in the module to ksp(...), and remember that the stubs stay until the last kapt processor leaves the module.

lab.title: Port a javac annotation processor to KSP
steps: Read JavacPackingSlipProcessor.java: the Java team's processor, given and read-only. Its process method makes four moves, and java-twins.txt shows the Java classes javac ran it on and the command. javac-packing-slip.txt is what it wrote: your target, byte for byte.

Read PackingSlipProcessor.kt. The provider, apiFeatures, the process wrapper and processSlip are given, in the same order as the Java process, and each comment names the javac line it replaces. Four functions are yours, one per move.
Run the tests: all five fail. Run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL09Kotlin -Pmine=l09: your port already runs in the real build and warns w: [ksp] l09 not done yet: 1. Find: ....

1. Check: write checkKind. A class passes; anything else gets logger.error on the symbol with the javac processor's words, @Inventory goes on a class, but Shape is an interface, plus one kind javac never sees: Van is an object.

1. Read: write slipLine. javac read the fields in source order and getAnnotation(Room.class); you read the primary constructor's properties in order, and the name argument of the @Room annotation. Check shortName first, then resolve the annotation type to be sure.
1. Write: write slipDependencies, aggregating, with the file of every class on the slip: the KSP form of the originating elements and of Gradle's aggregating category.

1. Prove: run the tests until all five pass. Run PortDemo with -Pmine=l09 and look for byte for byte: true. Then run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL09Kotlin -Pmine=l09, open labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l09/resources/META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt, and print it from the class path with ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.PackingSlipKt -Pmine=l09.

From memory: close both files and write, on paper, the KSP line for each of these javac calls: getElementsAnnotatedWith, printMessage(ERROR, text, element), getAnnotation(Room.class).name(), getOptions().get(key) and createResource(...). The drill below has the answer.
hints: Inventory::class.qualifiedName!! gives the full name that getSymbolsWithAnnotation needs; the short name finds nothing.
ClassKind.INTERFACE, ENUM_CLASS, ANNOTATION_CLASS and OBJECT match the Java processor's kindWords when you use the same words: an interface, an enum, an annotation, and an object for the new one.

cls.primaryConstructor?.parameters.orEmpty().filter { it.isVal || it.isVar } gives the properties in order. For @Room: annotations.firstOrNull { ... }?.arguments?.firstOrNull { it.name?.asString() == "name" }?.value as String?.
The first test compares bytes: a missing trailing newline or an extra space fails it. processSlip already writes the header and one \n per line; slipLine returns the line without its newline.
If the test that expects Shape.kt:6 fails, check that the error is logged on the symbol, not without one: a message without a symbol has no file and line.
lab.done: All five tests in PackingSlipProcessorTest pass, and PortDemo -Pmine=l09 prints the same, byte for byte: true.

drill.title: Port five javac lines from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write the KSP line for each javac line: (1) roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class), (2) messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, text, element), (3) type.getAnnotation(Room.class).name(), (4) processingEnv.getOptions().get("movemate.household"), (5) filer.createResource(StandardLocation.CLASS_OUTPUT, "", "META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt", elements). Which javac idea has no KSP line at all?

answer.html: // 1. Find resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") // 2. Check logger.error(text, symbol) // 3. Read an annotation argument cls.annotations.first { it.shortName.asString() == "Room" } .arguments.first { it.name?.asString() == "name" }.value as String // 4. Options environment.options["movemate.household"] // 5. Write a resource, aggregating, from every class's file codeGenerator.createNewFile(Dependencies(true, *files), "META-INF/movemate", "packing-slip", "txt") // no KSP line: claiming an annotation by returning true from process()

alt.title: JavacLines.java
alt.html: // The javac lines being ported roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class); // 1. Find messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, text, element); // 2. Check String room = type.getAnnotation(Room.class).name(); // 3. Read String household = processingEnv.getOptions().get("movemate.household"); // 4. Options filer.createResource(StandardLocation.CLASS_OUTPUT, "", "META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt", elements); // 5. Write return true; // claims @Inventory: KSP has no such thing

recap: Reflection inspects classes while the program runs. For four cards, its first call costs about as much as a generated card's, and each warm card about four to six times as much (some 190 to 280 ns against 45 ns here). It's fine for work that runs a few times on a few classes.
Generated code wins when the work repeats or a mistake should stop the build, and it needs no reflection setup in programs compiled ahead of time.

A processor only adds new files; writing a class again is a Redeclaration error. Jobs that change your classes (all-open, no-arg, kotlinx.serialization) belong to compiler plugins, and Arrow Optics, Koin and DataFrame now steer users from their KSP processors to plugins.

kapt runs Java-only processors on Java stubs of your classes, and the stubs are the cost. Swap kapt(...) for ksp(...) wherever a library ships a KSP processor, and keep kapt for the rest; one kapt processor keeps stubs in its module.

KSP2 is the only KSP since 2.3.0: not a compiler plugin, run in the Gradle daemon, versioned apart from Kotlin. In a multiplatform module, add the processor per target (kspJvm, kspJs, kspCommonMainMetadata); plain ksp(...) is an error.
The limit: no tool covers every job. KSP can't change a class, a compiler plugin changes it out of sight, reflection checks nothing until it runs, and kapt is slow.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "KSP is up to twice as fast as everything, so let's generate code for all our reflection and move every annotation library to KSP." Explain what you'd agree with, what you'd push back on, and how you'd decide each case.
explain.answer: The "up to 2x" is a 2021 Room benchmark of KSP against kapt, so it's about build time, and it compares two ways of running processors, not KSP with reflection. I'd agree with moving every library that ships a KSP processor from kapt to KSP: kapt writes Java stubs of every class in the module, and one kapt processor left keeps them there. I'd keep kapt only for processors that exist just for Java. On reflection I'd decide case by case. Our measurement showed a generated card is four to six times faster once warm, but that's a fifth of a microsecond, and the first calls were close. A debug screen or a settings read once at start doesn't need a processor and its module and tests. Code that runs constantly, or where a mistake should fail the build, is worth generating. And some jobs can't be done by KSP at all: anything that must change a class we wrote, like adding a member or removing final, needs a compiler plugin.

deeper.html:
Why are the first calls so close? Each first card makes the JVM link the card's string template: Kotlin compiles a template to a call through java.lang.invoke, and the JVM builds the code for each new kind of template the first time it runs. In the class log of the generated run, most of the hundred-odd classes loaded around the first card were java.lang.invoke classes, and reflection's first card needs the same machinery for its own templates, plus about twenty classes for reading annotations and fields. On a real program, reflection's start-up cost grows with the number of classes it inspects and with the libraries it drags in, which is what the Part 4 capstone measured.

Moshi offers both paths in one library and says when to pick which: "Prefer codegen for better performance and to avoid the kotlin-reflect dependency; prefer reflection to convert both private and protected properties." Its reflection adapter depends on kotlin-reflect, "a 2.5 MiB .jar file". This course's reflection cards avoid that by using plain Java reflection, which works for Kotlin classes because they compile to ordinary JVM classes, but sees only JVM facts: fields and their order, not Kotlin's nullability or default values.

The ecosystem moves both ways at once, and the reasons are the same picture. Libraries whose job is new code next to yours (Room's database code, Dagger's factories, kotlin-inject's components) went KSP-first or KSP-only. Libraries whose job is to change or extend your classes from the inside (Koin's wiring rewrites calls such as single<UserRepository>(), Arrow Optics needs companions, DataFrame adds properties) moved to compiler plugins, which also skip the per-target KSP configurations of multiplatform modules. Before you pick a library, read which of the two it has become.
